etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English towardes, from Old English tōweardes, tōwærdes, equivalent to toward +‎ -s (adverbial suffix).

quote.citation: 1835, Sir John Ross, Sir James Clark Ross, Narrative of a Second Voyage in Search of a North-west Passage …, Volume 1, pages 284–5:
quote.text: Towards the following morning, the thermometer fell to 5°; and at daylight, there was not an atom of water to be seen in any direction.

quote.citation: 1960 December, Voyageur, “The Mountain Railways of the Bernese Oberland”, in Trains Illustrated, page 752:
quote.text: To the left towers the Jungfrau, with the train heading directly towards it.

quote.citation: 2011 October 1, Phil McNulty, “Everton 0-2 Liverpool”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: But with Goodison Park openly directing its full hostility towards Atkinson, Liverpool went ahead when Carroll turned in his first Premier League goal of the season after 70 minutes.

definitions.definition: In the direction of something (indicated by context).

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto IV”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Thus as he spake, lo far away they spyde / A varlet running towards hastily  […]

definitions.definition: Near; at hand; in state of preparation; toward.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1595 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Romeo and Ivliet”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene v]:
quote.text: We have a trifling foolish banquet towards.
